question.text: \[ \mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} \textrm{i}-1 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix},\qquad C= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the vector $\mathbf{v}$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1+2\textrm{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PCP^{-1}.$
question.explanation:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where

\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \textrm{Re}(\mathbf{v}) & \textrm{Im}(\mathbf{v}) \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} ,\qquad C= \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Re}(\lambda) & \textrm{Im}(\lambda) \\ -\textrm{Im}(\lambda) & \textrm{Re}(\lambda) \end{bmatrix}, \]

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue $\lambda.$

First, notice that

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Re}(\lambda) & \textrm{Im}(\lambda) \\ -\textrm{Im}(\lambda) & \textrm{Re}(\lambda) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = C. \]

Next, we can find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{v} &=\begin{bmatrix} \textrm{i}-1 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} %\\[5pt] =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \color{blue}-1 \\ \color{blue}-3 \end{bmatrix}}_{\textrm{Re}(\mathbf{v})} + \textrm{i}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \color{red}1 \\ \color{red}0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{v})} \end{align*}

Finally, we can now construct $P\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} P &= \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \textrm{Re}(\mathbf{v}) & \textrm{Im}(\mathbf{v}) \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} %\\[5pt] =\begin{bmatrix} \color{blue}-1 & \color{red}1 \\ \color{blue}-3 & \color{red}0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: \[ \mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} -\textrm{i} \\ 2+3\textrm{i} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -6 \\ 6 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the vector $\mathbf{v}$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=1+6\textrm{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PCP^{-1}.$
question.explanation:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where

\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \textrm{Re}(\mathbf{v}) & \textrm{Im}(\mathbf{v}) \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} ,\qquad C= \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Re}(\lambda) & \textrm{Im}(\lambda) \\ -\textrm{Im}(\lambda) & \textrm{Re}(\lambda) \end{bmatrix}, \]

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue $\lambda.$

First, notice that

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Re}(\lambda) & \textrm{Im}(\lambda) \\ -\textrm{Im}(\lambda) & \textrm{Re}(\lambda) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ -6 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \neq C, \]

while

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Re}(\overline{\lambda}) & \textrm{Im}(\overline{\lambda}) \\ -\textrm{Im}(\overline{\lambda}) & \textrm{Re}(\overline{\lambda}) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -6 \\ 6 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = C. \]

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overline{\lambda}=1-6\textrm{i},$ the complex conjugate of $\lambda.$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overline{\mathbf{v}},$ the complex conjugate of $\mathbf{v}.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

\begin{align*} \overline{\mathbf{v}} &=\begin{bmatrix} \textrm{i} \\ 2-3\textrm{i} \end{bmatrix} %\\[5pt] =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\textrm{Re}(\overline{\mathbf{v}})} + \textrm{i}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}}_{\textrm{Im}(\overline{\mathbf{v}})} \end{align*}

Finally, we can now construct $P\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} P &= \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \textrm{Re}(\overline{\mathbf{v}}) & \textrm{Im}(\overline{\mathbf{v}}) \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} %\\[5pt] =\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: \[ \mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} 1+4\textrm{i} \\ -5\textrm{i} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the vector $\mathbf{v}$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=2-5\textrm{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PCP^{-1}.$
question.explanation:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where

\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \textrm{Re}(\mathbf{v}) & \textrm{Im}(\mathbf{v}) \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} ,\qquad C= \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Re}(\lambda) & \textrm{Im}(\lambda) \\ -\textrm{Im}(\lambda) & \textrm{Re}(\lambda) \end{bmatrix}, \]

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue $\lambda.$

First, notice that

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Re}(\lambda) & \textrm{Im}(\lambda) \\ -\textrm{Im}(\lambda) & \textrm{Re}(\lambda) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \neq C, \]

while

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Re}(\overline{\lambda}) & \textrm{Im}(\overline{\lambda}) \\ -\textrm{Im}(\overline{\lambda}) & \textrm{Re}(\overline{\lambda}) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = C. \]

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overline{\lambda}=2+5\textrm{i},$ the complex conjugate of $\lambda.$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overline{\mathbf{v}},$ the complex conjugate of $\mathbf{v}.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

\begin{align*} \overline{\mathbf{v}} &=\begin{bmatrix} 1-4\textrm{i} \\ 5\textrm{i} \end{bmatrix} %\\[5pt] =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\textrm{Re}(\overline{\mathbf{v}})} + \textrm{i}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}}_{\textrm{Im}(\overline{\mathbf{v}})} \end{align*}

Finally, we can now construct $P\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} P &= \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \textrm{Re}(\overline{\mathbf{v}}) & \textrm{Im}(\overline{\mathbf{v}}) \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} %\\[5pt] =\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

example.title: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Using the Complex Conjugate

question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} -7 & 5 \\ -10 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P=\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda=-2-5\textrm{i},$ and that $A=PCP^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of $ \dfrac{a^2+b^2}{c^2+d^2}? $
question.explanation:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where

\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \textrm{Re}(\mathbf{v}) & \textrm{Im}(\mathbf{v}) \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} ,\qquad C= \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Re}(\lambda) & \textrm{Im}(\lambda) \\ -\textrm{Im}(\lambda) & \textrm{Re}(\lambda) \end{bmatrix}, \]

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue $\lambda.$

Since we are given the eigenvalue $\lambda=-2-5\textrm{i},$ we can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

\[ C = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -5 \\ 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \]

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation \[ (A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}. \]

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =-2-5\textrm{i},$ and

\begin{align} A-\lambda I &= \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 5 \\ -10 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} -2-5\textrm{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2-5\textrm{i} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -5+5\textrm{i} & 5 \\ -10 & 5+5\textrm{i} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

\[ \begin{cases} (-5+5\textrm{i})x_1 + 5x_2 = 0 \\ -10x_1 +(5+5\textrm{i})x_2 = 0. \end{cases} \]

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

\[ x_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}(1+\textrm{i})x_2. \]

Hence, the general solution is given by

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2}(1+\textrm{i})x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{C}. \]

Setting $x_2=2$, we get the eigenvector

\[ \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1+\textrm{i} \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

\begin{align*} P &= \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert \\ \textrm{Re}(\mathbf{v}) & \textrm{Im}(\mathbf{v}) \\ \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Finally, \[ \dfrac{a^2+b^2}{c^2+d^2}=\dfrac{1^2+1^2}{2^2+0^2}=\dfrac{1}{2}. \]
